reflection.theme: The quiet weekend as proof of life
reflection.quote: The world breaks everyone, and afterward many are strong at the broken places.
reflection.reading:
Saturday morning in early September has a particular quality to it. The light is starting to slant differently, summer loosening its grip. If you're new to this, a Saturday can feel like a test — a whole open day with no scaffolding, no work to hide behind. The old version of you knew exactly what to do with it. The new one is still figuring it out.

What I've learned, eleven years in, is that the ordinary Saturday is the actual prize. Coffee that tastes like coffee. A hike, a long breakfast with someone you love, a book you don't have to reread because you were blacked out the first time. Errands. A nap. The stuff I used to consider a waste of a weekend turned out to be the whole point. My twenty-two-year-old self would have called this small. He was wrong. He was calling it small because he couldn't feel it.

Hemingway's line gets quoted a lot, usually to make suffering sound noble. I don't read it that way. I read it as a fact. You broke. You're mending. The strength shows up in the unremarkable places — the Saturday you didn't blow up, the morning you woke up clear, the phone call you actually remember. That's the strong at the broken places. That's today.
reflection.meditation: Sit for two minutes with the day in front of you. Not the whole weekend, not next week. Just today. What's one small ordinary thing you get to do sober that you couldn't do drunk? Start there.

affirmations: I am building a life I don't need to escape from.
Today I get to be present for the small, ordinary hours — and that's the point.
I am strong in the places I used to break.

gratitude.prayer: Grateful for a clear Saturday morning and a body that isn't paying for last night. Grateful for the people who stuck around while I figured this out, and for the ones I've met since who only know me sober. Grateful that ordinary now feels like enough — because for a long time nothing was.
gratitude.closing: One more day. That's the whole deal.
